The corner ordering follows the standard Marching Cubes convention (typically 0-7 corresponding to binary indices of corner presence) [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly provides the code for `get_cube_indices`, which calculates the marching cubes case index using the formula: `cube_indices[:, 0] * 1 | cube_indices[:, 1] * 2 | ... | cube_indices[:, 7] * 128`. This corresponds exactly to the standard Marching Cubes convention where the corner index (0-7) serves as the binary bit position for the case index (binary indices of corner presence).

For each voxel $i$ at `coords[i]`, determine the integer coordinates of its 8 corners [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that for each voxel $i$ at `coords[i]`, one determines the integer coordinates of its 8 corners. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly describes the `sparse_marching_cubes` function which takes `coords` (integer coordinates of active voxels) and `corners` (scalar values at the 8 corners of each voxel). Furthermore, the `sparse_marching_cubes_from_points` function is described as gathering the 8 corner values for each voxel dynamically based on the provided integer coordinates. The standard definition of a voxel at integer coordinates $(x, y, z)$ implies its corners are at the integer coordinates surrounding that point (e.g., $(x,y,z)$ to $(x+1,y+1,z+1)$). The evidence supports the process of using voxel coordinates to identify and process the 8 corners associated with each voxel.
